description: Test your knowledge of PA H7 | Benign Leukocytosis & Leukemias.

cards.text: What is the normal total leucocyte count (TLC) range in a healthy adult, and what defines leucocytosis?
cards.answer: Normal TLC: 4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L. Leucocytosis = TLC > 11 × 10⁹/L. Leucopenia = TLC < 4.0 × 10⁹/L.

cards.text: Define neutrophilia and state the absolute neutrophil count threshold.
cards.answer: Neutrophilia is an absolute neutrophil count > 7.5 × 10⁹/L. It reflects either increased marrow output, demargination, or reduced apoptosis.

cards.text: Name three common pathological causes of neutrophilia and explain the mechanism.
cards.answer: Bacterial infection (G-CSF/IL-8 release), inflammatory/tissue necrosis (MI, burns, surgery), steroid therapy (impairs margination). All trigger cytokine-mediated marrow release.

tip.tip: Infection #1 worldwide; think inflammation and stress

cards.text: What is a 'left shift' and what does it indicate clinically?
cards.answer: Presence of immature granulocytes (bands, metamyelocytes, myelocytes) in peripheral blood due to premature marrow release. Indicates severe infection or tissue injury.

tip.tip: Immature cells 'shift left' on an automated differential

cards.text: Distinguish toxic granulation from Döhle bodies. When are they seen together?
cards.answer: Toxic granulation: enlarged, darkly staining primary granules from accelerated granulopoiesis. Döhle bodies: pale cytoplasmic inclusions of rough ER remnants. Both appear in severe sepsis, burns, and pregnancy—not in CML (unlike Auer rods).

tip.tip: Toxic = dark granules; Döhle = pale ER inclusions; both = stress response

cards.text: Define a leukaemoid reaction and name two common causes.
cards.answer: Reactive leucocytosis (>50 × 10⁹/L) with marked left shift that mimics leukaemia but is not malignant. Causes: miliary TB, severe pneumonia, severe haemolysis, metastatic carcinoma.

tip.tip: Leukaemoid = looks like leukaemia but isn't; always benign reactive

cards.text: How does the LAP score help differentiate a leukaemoid reaction from chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML)?
cards.answer: LAP (leucocyte alkaline phosphatase) score is HIGH (↑↑) in leukaemoid reaction and LOW or absent in CML. This is the classic differentiating test.

tip.tip: High LAP = benign reactive; Low LAP = suspect CML

cards.text: What is a leukoerythroblastic reaction and when does it occur?
cards.answer: Presence of nucleated red blood cells (NRBCs) in peripheral blood alongside a left shift of neutrophils. Indicates severe marrow stress from infection, haemolysis, or major tissue injury.

tip.tip: Leuko-erythro = both WBCs and RBCs released prematurely
